records.name: Desert Cottontail
records.diet: Grasses, mesquite, cactus pads, and other desert plants
records.shelter: Brush cover and borrowed or natural burrows
records.preferredHabitat: Brushy flats with shade and open forage
records.fact: Desert cottontails get most of their water from the plants they eat.

requirements.hint: Brush for cover and a burrow bank to shelter in.

records.role: A common desert herbivore that grazes grasses and browse. It is a cornerstone prey species, feeding foxes, coyotes, bobcats, and raptors. Its abundance helps support the desert's predators.

records.name: Kit Fox
records.diet: Kangaroo rats, rabbits, insects, and occasional fruit
records.shelter: Cool underground dens with several entrances
records.preferredHabitat: Open desert with abundant small prey
records.fact: The smallest wild dog in North America, its huge ears both hear prey and shed heat.

requirements.hint: Kit foxes return when prey is plentiful and dens are ready.

records.role: A small nocturnal desert canid and mesopredator that hunts rodents and rabbits. It seldom needs to drink, getting moisture from prey. Coyotes are its main threat.

records.name: Coyote
records.diet: Rodents, rabbits, fruit, carrion, and insects
records.shelter: Brushy washes and rock dens
records.preferredHabitat: Open desert with prey and cover
records.fact: The most vocal wild mammal in North America; a howling pack sounds like many more.

requirements.hint: Cover, shade, and prey on the move.

records.role: The desert's most adaptable predator, an omnivore taking rodents, rabbits, fruit, and carrion. It is the top mammalian predator here and the main killer of kit foxes. Its howls carry for miles at dusk.

records.name: Kangaroo Rat
records.diet: Seeds, carefully cached underground
records.shelter: Deep burrow systems in loose soil
records.preferredHabitat: Loose soil below seed-bearing brush
records.fact: Kangaroo rats never sweat or pant and get by on water made from the dry seeds they eat.

requirements.hint: Burrow banks and seed plants nearby.

records.role: A seed-eating rodent and key desert prey species. It caches seeds underground, shaping which plants grow. It feeds nearly every desert predator, from rattlesnakes to owls to foxes.

records.name: Black-tailed Jackrabbit
records.diet: Grasses, cactus, and woody twigs and bark
records.shelter: Shade forms scraped under brush
records.preferredHabitat: Open flats with scattered brush
records.fact: A jackrabbit's enormous ears act like radiators, releasing body heat to keep it cool.

requirements.hint: Open running room with brush for shade.

records.role: A fast, open-country herbivore that browses grasses, twigs, and cactus. It is major prey for coyotes, bobcats, and large raptors. Its big ears both hear predators and dump heat.

records.name: Greater Roadrunner
records.diet: Lizards, insects, scorpions, and small snakes
records.shelter: Low nests in brush and cactus
records.preferredHabitat: Open hunting ground with brushy edges
records.fact: It slams large prey against rocks to break the bones, and will kill and eat rattlesnakes.

requirements.hint: Open desert, brush, and reptile prey about.

records.role: A ground-running predatory bird that sprints down lizards, insects, scorpions, and snakes. It is a key mesopredator on small desert reptiles and arthropods. Coyotes and hawks hunt it.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Greater Roadrunner

records.name: Burrowing Owl
records.diet: Insects and small rodents
records.shelter: Underground burrows dug by other animals
records.preferredHabitat: Burrow mounds with open hunting space
records.fact: It hisses a raspy call that mimics a rattlesnake to scare intruders out of its burrow.

requirements.hint: Ready-made burrows and open ground to hunt over.

records.role: A small ground-dwelling owl that nests in borrowed burrows and hunts insects by day and rodents at night. It is both an insectivore and a mesopredator on small mammals. Badgers and coyotes prey on it.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Burrowing Owl

records.name: Gambel's Quail
records.diet: Seeds, leaves, and cactus fruit
records.shelter: Dense brush thickets
records.preferredHabitat: Brushy cover with seed plants
records.fact: A male sentinel calls from a perch while the rest of the covey feeds below.

requirements.hint: Thick brush to hide a whole covey.

records.role: A social, ground-feeding quail that eats seeds, greens, and cactus fruit. It is important prey for coyotes, bobcats, and desert hawks. Coveys post a lookout while the flock forages.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Gambel's Quail

records.name: Desert Tortoise
records.diet: Grasses, wildflowers, and cactus pads
records.shelter: Long, cool burrows
records.preferredHabitat: Native plants with shade and burrow ground
records.fact: Desert tortoises can live 80 years and spend up to 98% of their lives in burrows.

requirements.hint: Shade, native plants, and burrow habitat.

records.role: A long-lived herbivore and ecosystem engineer. Its burrows, which can exceed 10 metres, shelter snakes, lizards, rodents, and insects. Adults are nearly predator-free, but eggs and young are widely eaten.

records.name: Horned Lizard
records.diet: Mostly ants, plus other small insects
records.shelter: Loose sand and rock edges
records.preferredHabitat: Sunny open ground near ant trails
records.fact: Texas horned lizards can squirt a jet of blood from their eyes to startle predators.

requirements.hint: Sunny rocks and sandy ground bring the ants — and the lizards.

records.role: A specialist insectivore that feeds mainly on harvester ants, with a large stomach to process them. It is prey for roadrunners, hawks, shrikes, and snakes. Its blood-squirting defense targets canid predators.

records.name: Collared Lizard
records.diet: Insects and smaller lizards
records.shelter: Rock piles and ledges
records.preferredHabitat: Boulder fields with lookout rocks
records.fact: Collared lizards sprint on their hind legs like tiny dinosaurs, tail streaming behind.

requirements.hint: Plenty of warm rock to perch and hunt from.

records.role: An active, sit-and-wait predator of insects and smaller lizards among the rocks. It is a mesopredator on desert arthropods and hatchling reptiles. Hawks, snakes, and roadrunners prey on it.

records.name: Western Rattlesnake
records.diet: Rodents and small mammals
records.shelter: Rock crevices and burrows
records.preferredHabitat: Rocky shelter near busy rodent trails
records.fact: It adds a rattle segment at each shed, but segments break, so you can't count its age.

requirements.hint: Rocky shelter and rodents to hunt.

records.role: A venomous ambush predator and key control on desert rodent populations. It swallows prey whole and eats only every few weeks. Roadrunners, hawks, and coyotes are among its predators.

records.name: Desert Tarantula
records.diet: Insects and other small invertebrates
records.shelter: Silk-lined ground burrows
records.preferredHabitat: Undisturbed ground with burrow banks
records.fact: A desert tarantula may live 25 years, most of it within a few feet of one burrow.

requirements.hint: Quiet, diggable ground.

records.role: A long-lived, nocturnal ambush predator of insects and other invertebrates from its burrow. It is a mesopredator on desert arthropods. Birds, snakes, and the tarantula hawk wasp prey on it.

records.name: Desert Scorpion
records.diet: Insects, spiders, and other small invertebrates
records.shelter: Burrows and cover under rocks and bark
records.preferredHabitat: Rocky cover with night hunting ground
records.fact: Scorpions glow blue-green under ultraviolet light, and no one is entirely sure why.

requirements.hint: Rocks to hide beneath by day.

records.role: The largest scorpion in North America, a nocturnal ambush predator of insects, spiders, and even other scorpions. It is a mesopredator on desert arthropods and small prey. Owls, lizards, and roadrunners hunt it.

records.name: Desert Bee
records.diet: Cactus flower nectar and pollen
records.shelter: Tiny solitary ground nests
records.preferredHabitat: Blooming cactus and brush
records.fact: Solitary cactus bees nest alone but gather by the thousands in shared ground colonies.

requirements.hint: Cactus blooms are the desert's flower patch.

records.role: A solitary native bee and key pollinator of desert cacti such as prickly pear and cholla. As a herbivore on nectar and pollen, it sustains cactus reproduction. Lizards, birds, and spiders prey on it.

records.name: Mountain Goat
records.diet: Alpine grasses, sedges, forbs, woody browse, mosses, and lichens
records.shelter: Shallow bedding depressions pawed into cliff ledges and rocky terrain
records.preferredHabitat: Steep alpine and subalpine cliffs with escape terrain above turf
records.fact: Both sexes grow permanent black horns; you can count the annual rings to age one.

requirements.hint: Rocky terrain and restored alpine vegetation.

records.role: A sure-footed alpine grazer of the highest cliffs, browsing grasses, forbs, and lichens across the rock. Its rubbery-padded hooves grip terrain few predators can follow. Kids and adults are still taken by cougars, and eagles snatch newborns from ledges.

records.name: Bighorn Sheep
records.diet: Chiefly grasses and sedges, with forbs and woody browse in winter
records.shelter: Beds on rocky ledges and rugged escape terrain near cliffs
records.preferredHabitat: Open grassy mountain slopes beside rugged, rocky cliffs
records.fact: Bighorns flee across rocky ledges barely a few inches wide to escape predators.

requirements.hint: Grassy slopes with rocky escape ground.

records.role: A cliff-edge grazer that crops grasses and forbs on open slopes, never far from rugged escape terrain. Rams clash horns in booming rutting contests each fall. Lambs and adults are hunted by cougars, and eagles may take the very young.

records.name: American Pika
records.diet: Grasses, forbs, and wildflowers, gathered and dried into winter haypiles
records.shelter: Cool gaps deep within talus and broken rock
records.preferredHabitat: Talus slopes and rock piles bordering alpine flower meadows
records.fact: Pikas cut and sun-dry little haystacks of plants to eat beneath the winter snow.

requirements.hint: Cool rock piles and flowers to harvest.

records.role: A tiny talus-dwelling relative of rabbits and the engine of the alpine food web. It spends summer harvesting haypiles of forbs and grasses to survive under snow. Pikas are hunted by weasels, martens, foxes, and eagles alike.

records.name: Yellow-bellied Marmot
records.diet: Grasses, flowering plants, and seeds in late summer
records.shelter: Deep burrow systems dug beneath boulders
records.preferredHabitat: Open meadow patches with boulders and burrow ground
records.fact: Predation causes about 98% of yellow-bellied marmots' summer deaths.

requirements.hint: Burrows, meadow patches, and open space.

records.role: A stout, sun-loving rodent that grazes meadow plants and fattens on seeds before an eight-month hibernation. Colonies whistle alarm calls from boulder lookouts. They are prime prey for golden eagles, coyotes, and foxes.

records.name: Snowshoe Hare
records.diet: Green plants in summer; buds, twigs, bark, and conifer needles in winter
records.shelter: Shallow forms under dense shrubs and conifer cover
records.preferredHabitat: Brushy thickets and dense understory near open turf
records.fact: Its molt from brown to winter white is triggered by day length, not snow.

requirements.hint: Cover and forage at the treeline.

records.role: A browsing hare of brushy treeline cover whose coat flips brown-to-white with the seasons. Its numbers cycle roughly every ten years, driving predator populations. Martens, foxes, eagles, and owls all hunt it.

sources.name: USFS Fire Effects Information System - Lepus americanus

records.name: Elk
records.diet: Grasses, sedges, and forbs in summer; browse, bark, and lichens in winter
records.shelter: Beds in timber edges and shaded cover beside meadows
records.preferredHabitat: High summer meadows near forest cover and snowmelt water
records.fact: Elk chase the 'green wave' of new growth up the mountains each summer.

requirements.hint: High meadow forage and snowmelt water.

records.role: A large migratory grazer that summers in high meadows, following fresh growth uphill and bugling through the autumn rut. Bulls regrow massive antlers yearly. Cougars take adults, while eagles and coyotes may take newborn calves.

records.name: Mule Deer
records.diet: A selective browser of shrubs, forbs, buds, fruits, and lichens
records.shelter: Beds in shaded thickets and krummholz cover
records.preferredHabitat: High summer meadows and shrublands with clean water
records.fact: Mule deer clear obstacles with a bounding, four-footed gait called stotting.

requirements.hint: Forage and clean water up high.

records.role: A selective high-country browser that summers in alpine meadows and shrublands before migrating down each fall. It picks the most digestible forbs, buds, and browse. Cougars are its main predator; fawns are also taken by eagles and coyotes.

records.name: Red Fox
records.diet: Voles, pikas, hares, ground birds and eggs, insects, and berries
records.shelter: Earthen dens, often burrows co-opted from other animals
records.preferredHabitat: High country with rocky cover and abundant small prey
records.fact: Red foxes often move into burrows dug by rabbits or marmots instead of digging.

requirements.hint: Foxes follow the pikas and marmots.

records.role: An adaptable mountain mesopredator that hunts pikas, marmots, and ground birds and rounds out its diet with insects and berries. It listens for prey moving beneath the snow, then dives in headfirst. Golden eagles are its main threat here.

records.name: Pine Marten
records.diet: Voles, red squirrels, pikas, hares, birds, eggs, insects, and berries
records.shelter: Dens in tree cavities, hollow logs, stumps, and rock crevices
records.preferredHabitat: Structurally complex treeline forest with rocky cover
records.fact: Pine martens hunt beneath the winter snowpack through tunnels others can't reach.

requirements.hint: Rocky cover and prey near the treeline.

records.role: An agile treeline weasel that hunts voles, squirrels, pikas, and young hares, adding berries and insects in season. It ranges over complex forest and rock, even beneath the snowpack. Great horned owls, eagles, and larger carnivores prey on it.

sources.name: Alaska Dept. of Fish & Game - American Marten

records.name: White-tailed Ptarmigan
records.diet: Buds, twigs, leaves, seeds, and flowers; willow is the sole winter food
records.shelter: Camouflaged ground scrapes among lichen-covered alpine rocks
records.preferredHabitat: Alpine tundra above treeline year-round, wintering in willow basins
records.fact: It is the only North American bird living entirely above treeline all year.

requirements.hint: Alpine shrubs and quiet nesting cover, with hardy frostflowers in bloom.

records.role: A superbly camouflaged alpine grouse that grazes buds, leaves, and seeds, surviving winter almost entirely on willow. It grows feathered 'snowshoes' on its feet each winter. Eagles, foxes, weasels, and martens all hunt it and its chicks.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - White-tailed Ptarmigan

records.name: Clark's Nutcracker
records.diet: Pine seeds cached by the thousand, plus insects and small animals
records.shelter: Cup nest in conifer branches, sited near winter seed caches
records.preferredHabitat: High conifer forest and treeline near pine-seed sources
records.fact: It can relocate thousands of buried seed caches months later, even under snow.

requirements.hint: A recovering treeline with seeds to cache.

records.role: A mountain corvid that harvests and buries thousands of pine seeds, replanting the very forests it depends on. Its cached hoard lets it breed in deep winter. It also takes insects and small vertebrates when available.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - Clark's Nutcracker

records.name: Golden Eagle
records.diet: Marmots, hares, ground squirrels, ptarmigan and other birds, plus carrion
records.shelter: Huge stick eyries on cliffs and steep escarpments
records.preferredHabitat: Open, high country with cliffs and abundant medium prey
records.fact: Golden eagles sometimes line their nests with aromatic leaves, perhaps to deter insects.

requirements.hint: Eagles arrive last — when the high country is truly alive again.

records.role: The apex hunter of the high country, taking marmots, hares, and ptarmigan and even smaller carnivores in powerful stoops. It arrives only when the mountain teems with prey. Adults have essentially no predators.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - Golden Eagle
Birds of the World - Golden Eagle Food Habits

records.name: Alpine Butterfly
records.diet: Larvae eat stonecrop; adults sip nectar from Sedum and daisy-family flowers
records.shelter: No nest; larvae shelter in leaf litter and rocks, overwintering as eggs
records.preferredHabitat: Rocky open alpine and montane slopes where stonecrop grows
records.fact: Its pale red-and-black wings warn predators that it tastes unpalatable.

requirements.hint: Alpine flowers in bloom.

records.role: A hardy alpine butterfly whose caterpillars feed only on stonecrop while adults nectar across the meadow flowers. Its aposematic wings advertise a foul taste. Birds and spiders that ignore the warning still catch some.

sources.name: Butterflies and Moths of North America - Parnassius smintheus

records.name: Alpine Bumblebee
records.diet: Nectar and pollen from deep-throated alpine flowers
records.shelter: Colonial nests in ground cavities and old rodent burrows
records.preferredHabitat: High alpine and boreal flower meadows, often above treeline
records.fact: This bee's tongue grew measurably shorter from 1966 to 2014 as flowers declined.

requirements.hint: More flowers, more bees — even up here.

records.role: A cold-tolerant, long-tongued bumblebee that pollinates deep alpine blossoms, shivering its flight muscles to fly in near-freezing air. Its colonies nest underground. Birds, crab spiders, and robber flies prey on foragers.

sources.name: Molecular Ecology - Alpine bumblebee tongue-length study

records.name: Cutthroat Trout
records.diet: Aquatic and terrestrial insects; larger fish add small fish to the diet
records.shelter: Cold, clear pools and undercut banks; gravel riffles for spawning
records.preferredHabitat: Cold, clear, connected snowmelt streams and mountain lakes
records.fact: A poor competitor, native cutthroat are displaced by introduced brown and brook trout.

requirements.hint: Cold, clean, connected snowmelt pools.

records.role: A cold-water native whose presence signals a clean, healthy mountain stream. It picks off drifting insects and, when large, smaller fish. It is threatened by non-native trout that out-compete and prey on it.

records.name: Shore Crab
records.diet: Mostly algae, plus detritus, worms, snails, and carrion
records.shelter: Tidepool rocks and crevices
records.preferredHabitat: Rocky tidepools and intertidal splash zone
records.fact: Striped shore crabs graze algae but will scavenge and even turn cannibal after molting.

requirements.hint: Restore the tidepools and the crabs scuttle back first.

records.role: An abundant intertidal grazer-scavenger that keeps rock surfaces clear of algae and recycles carrion. It is a key prey item for gulls, shorebirds, and larger crabs, linking algae to higher predators.

records.name: Hermit Crab
records.diet: Algae, detritus, and scavenged carrion
records.shelter: Borrowed empty snail shells
records.preferredHabitat: Tidepools with a supply of empty shells
records.fact: When a better shell appears, hermit crabs line up by size and swap shells down the chain.

requirements.hint: Tidepools plus washed-up shells to move into.

records.role: A tidepool scavenger that cleans up algae and carrion and recycles empty snail shells as portable armor. It is common prey for gulls, fish, and octopus in the intertidal food web.

records.name: Ochre Sea Star
records.diet: Mussels, barnacles, limpets, chitons, and snails
records.shelter: Tidepool rock faces and crevices
records.preferredHabitat: Wave-washed rocky intertidal with shellfish
records.fact: The classic keystone predator: removing it lets mussels overrun the whole shore.

requirements.hint: Sea stars need established pools with mussels to eat.

records.role: The textbook keystone predator of the rocky shore. By eating mussels it sets the mussel bed's lower limit and keeps space open for many other species, maintaining intertidal biodiversity.

records.name: Giant Green Anemone
records.diet: Crabs, detached mussels, and small fish stung by its tentacles
records.shelter: Tidepool walls, often below mussel beds
records.preferredHabitat: Clear, surge-fed tidepools near mussel beds
records.fact: Its green glow comes from algae living inside its tissues that share sugars.

requirements.hint: Clear, quiet pools.

records.role: A sit-and-wait carnivore of tidepools that ambushes prey washed off the rocks, while also farming symbiotic algae for extra food. It is a minor predator that helps recycle dislodged shellfish and crabs.

sources.name: Monterey Bay Aquarium - Giant green anemone

records.name: California Mussel
records.diet: Plankton filtered from seawater
records.shelter: Dense beds anchored to wave-washed rock
records.preferredHabitat: Exposed rocky shore with clean moving water
records.fact: A single mussel filters several liters of seawater an hour as it feeds.

requirements.hint: Clean water over rocky shore.

records.role: A reef-building filter feeder whose beds create habitat for countless small animals. It is the key prey that ties together the shore's top predators, from ochre sea stars to sea otters and oystercatchers.

records.name: Pacific Littleneck Clam
records.diet: Plankton filtered from seawater
records.shelter: Buried in sand and gravel
records.preferredHabitat: Stable sand and gravel near tidepools
records.fact: You can estimate a littleneck clam's age by counting the growth rings on its shell.

requirements.hint: Stable, quiet sand to dig into.

records.role: A buried filter feeder that helps clean coastal water and stores energy in sheltered sediment. It is important prey for sea otters, shorebirds, crabs, and gulls that dig or crack it open.

sources.name: Animal Diversity Web - Enhydra lutris (predation on clams)

records.name: Snowy Plover
records.diet: Sand crustaceans, mole crabs, and kelp-fly larvae
records.shelter: Shallow scrapes hidden on open sand
records.preferredHabitat: Undisturbed sandy beaches and dune edges
records.fact: Snowy plover chicks can run and feed themselves within hours of hatching.

requirements.hint: Anchored dunes and a protected stretch of quiet beach.

records.role: A small beach forager that snaps up tiny crustaceans and kelp flies along the tide line. A threatened species and sensitive indicator of quiet, undisturbed beach; its nests fail easily where beaches are busy.

sources.name: All About Birds - Snowy Plover Life History

records.name: Western Gull
records.diet: Fish, crabs, clams, sea stars, and carrion
records.shelter: Open beach, rocky points, and islands
records.preferredHabitat: Any shoreline with food to scavenge or catch
records.fact: Western gulls crack clams by dropping them from the air onto rocks below.

requirements.hint: Gulls show up as soon as there's a beach worth patrolling.

records.role: A bold generalist that scavenges carrion and preys on crabs, shellfish, and even sea stars, cleaning the beach and linking many prey to the top of the food web. Foxes and coyotes take gulls and their eggs on land.

sources.name: All About Birds - Western Gull Life History

records.name: Brown Pelican
records.diet: Small schooling fish, especially anchovies
records.shelter: Quiet roosts on rocks and sandbars
records.preferredHabitat: Fish-rich nearshore water with quiet roosts
records.fact: Brown pelicans plunge-dive from up to 65 feet, twisting to protect the neck on impact.

requirements.hint: Quiet roosting space and fishable water.

records.role: A plunge-diving fish specialist whose recovery after DDT is a major conservation success. Its presence signals healthy schools of forage fish like anchovies in nearshore water.

sources.name: All About Birds - Brown Pelican Life History

records.name: Pelagic Cormorant
records.diet: Small fish, plus crabs and shrimp chased underwater
records.shelter: Cliff and rock roosts
records.preferredHabitat: Rocky shore with clear diving water
records.fact: Cormorant feathers soak through on purpose, so less buoyancy makes them better divers.

requirements.hint: Healthy rocky shallows to dive in.

records.role: A pursuit-diving fish hunter that works rocky reefs and the water column. It depends on clear water and healthy fish stocks, so thriving cormorants signal a productive rocky shore.

sources.name: All About Birds - Pelagic Cormorant Life History

records.name: Green Sea Turtle
records.diet: Mostly seagrass and algae as adults; omnivorous when young
records.shelter: Offshore waters; nests on quiet sand
records.preferredHabitat: Clean shallow water with seagrass and undisturbed beach
records.fact: Green sea turtles return to nest on the very beach where they hatched decades earlier.

requirements.hint: An undisturbed nesting beach and clean water.

records.role: The only mostly herbivorous sea turtle; adults graze seagrass and algae, keeping beds healthy, while juveniles start as omnivores. Its nesting success is a strong indicator of clean water and undisturbed beaches.

records.name: Harbor Seal
records.diet: Fish, plus squid, octopus, and crustaceans
records.shelter: Quiet haul-out beaches and rocks
records.preferredHabitat: Calm, clean water with undisturbed haul-out shore
records.fact: Harbor seals can sleep underwater, surfacing to breathe without fully waking.

requirements.hint: Quiet beaches and clean water — seals need calm above all.

records.role: A generalist marine predator that eats whatever fish is abundant and easy to catch. Sharks and killer whales are its main predators offshore, but on this restored coast it sits near the top of the food web.

records.name: Sea Otter
records.diet: Sea urchins, crabs, mussels, clams, and other shellfish
records.shelter: Kelp canopy anchor points
records.preferredHabitat: Kelp forest and rocky shore with abundant shellfish
records.fact: Sea otters wrap up in kelp before sleeping so they don't drift away.

requirements.hint: Kelp habitat and shellfish beds first; otters follow.

records.role: A keystone species: by eating sea urchins it stops them overgrazing kelp, letting kelp forests and the life they shelter thrive. It also preys heavily on mussels and clams along the rocky shore.

records.name: Bottlenose Dolphin
records.diet: Fish, squid, and crustaceans
records.shelter: Open coastal water
records.preferredHabitat: Clean, lively nearshore water
records.fact: Bottlenose dolphins call each other by name, using signature whistles unique to each one.

requirements.hint: A clean, busy shoreline brings dolphins close in.

records.role: A clever, cooperative predator that herds fish and hunts squid in nearshore water. Larger sharks and orcas can prey on it, but in this roster it is a top predator whose presence marks a lively, fish-rich coast.

records.name: Gray Whale
records.diet: Amphipods and other tiny bottom crustaceans, sifted from sediment
records.shelter: Open ocean; passes close to healthy shores
records.preferredHabitat: Seen offshore from a fully restored coast
records.fact: Gray whales migrate up to 14,000 miles round trip, among the longest of any mammal.

requirements.hint: Only a truly thriving shore earns a whale sighting. Watch the horizon.

records.role: A bottom-feeding baleen whale that rolls on its side to suck up sediment and filter out tiny crustaceans. Killer whales are its main predator; a passing gray whale is a sign of a fully restored, productive coast.

records.name: American Goldfinch
records.diet: Almost entirely seeds — thistle, sunflower, aster, and grass seeds
records.shelter: Tightly woven cup nest lashed high in a shrub with spider silk
records.preferredHabitat: Weedy fields and open areas with thistle, sunflower, and asters
records.fact: Goldfinches are strict vegetarians and nest late in summer so thistle down is ready to line their nests.

requirements.hint: Plant a wildflower patch and add a bird perch.

records.role: A specialist granivore that thrives on thistle and other composite seeds, making it an important disperser of weedy plant seeds across the meadow. Being small and abundant, it is prey for agile bird-hunting hawks and small owls.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — American Goldfinch Life History

records.name: Eastern Bluebird
records.diet: Mainly ground insects (caterpillars, beetles, grasshoppers); fruit in winter
records.shelter: Grass-lined nest inside tree cavities, old woodpecker holes, or boxes
records.preferredHabitat: Grassy openings with scattered trees and perches to hunt from
records.fact: Eastern Bluebirds can spot a tiny insect in the grass from about 60 feet away, then drop down to grab it.

requirements.hint: Native grass, a berry bush, and a perch to hunt from.

records.role: A cavity-nesting insectivore that hunts caterpillars, beetles, and grasshoppers from perches, switching to berries in winter, both controlling insects and dispersing fruit seeds. It competes for nest holes and is preyed on by hawks and small owls.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Eastern Bluebird Life History

records.name: Leafcutter Bee
records.diet: Adults eat nectar and pollen from many flowering plants
records.shelter: Nests in hollow stems and soil, lining cells with cut leaf pieces
records.preferredHabitat: Meadows and gardens with diverse flowers and nesting cavities
records.fact: Female leafcutter bees snip neat circles from leaves to build and seal their nest cells.

requirements.hint: Clover and wildflowers side by side.

records.role: A solitary native bee that pollinates a wide range of meadow and crop plants, carrying pollen on the underside of its abdomen. Its leaf-lined nest cells provision the next generation with pollen and nectar. Adults are caught by ambush predators and aerial insectivores.

sources.name: USDA Forest Service — Leafcutter Bees (Megachile spp.)

records.name: Painted Lady
records.diet: Adults nectar on composite flowers; caterpillars eat thistles and mallows
records.shelter: Rests on vegetation; caterpillars build silk nests on host plants
records.preferredHabitat: Open meadows and disturbed ground with thistles and nectar flowers
records.fact: Painted ladies migrate thousands of miles across continents — one of the most widespread butterflies on Earth.

requirements.hint: Butterfly flowers near a clover patch.

records.role: A wide-ranging migratory butterfly and generalist nectar pollinator whose caterpillars feed on thistles, mallows, and over 100 other host plants. Population booms can trigger massive migrations. Adults and larvae are eaten by birds, wasps, and spiders.

sources.name: Butterflies and Moths of North America — Painted Lady

records.name: American Badger
records.diet: Digs out ground squirrels, gophers, voles, and mice; also insects
records.shelter: Digs its own large underground burrows; a powerful excavator
records.preferredHabitat: Open meadows and grasslands with diggable soil and rodent prey
records.fact: Badgers sometimes team up with coyotes: the badger digs prey out below while the coyote catches those that bolt above ground.

requirements.hint: Brush pile and rock pile, once voles have returned.

records.role: A fossorial carnivore that hunts by digging burrowing rodents straight out of their tunnels, keeping ground squirrel and vole numbers down. Its abandoned burrows benefit other animals. Adult badgers have essentially no predators in this meadow.

records.name: Pileated Woodpecker
records.diet: Carpenter ants and wood-boring beetle larvae; also termites, berries, and nuts
records.shelter: Excavates a new rectangular nest cavity each year in large dead snags
records.preferredHabitat: Mature and old-growth forest with big standing snags and downed logs
records.fact: Its deep rectangular excavations can be large enough to snap a small tree in half.

requirements.hint: Standing deadwood beside a nesting tree.

records.role: The pileated woodpecker is a keystone ecosystem engineer whose big cavities become homes for wood ducks, flying squirrels, fishers, bats, and barred owls. It regulates carpenter ant and beetle populations and opens decaying wood to fungi and decomposers. It sits as a secondary consumer and feeds raptors and mustelids.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Pileated Woodpecker

records.name: Pacific Wren
records.diet: Beetles, caterpillars, ants, flies, spiders, and millipedes; some winter berries
records.shelter: Domed nests low in upturned roots, decaying logs, and stream banks
records.preferredHabitat: Old-growth conifer forest with dense understory near streams
records.fact: Pacific wren numbers along streams rise with salmon runs, whose nutrients boost the insects the wrens eat.

requirements.hint: Ferns and a mushroom log in the shade.

records.role: The Pacific wren is a secondary consumer that suppresses understory invertebrates in old-growth forest, passing that energy up to hawks, corvids, and weasels. Its dependence on damp, log-strewn old growth and salmon-fed streams makes it a living indicator of both forest and watershed health. It nests low in root tangles and rotting wood.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Pacific Wren

records.name: Rough-skinned Newt
records.diet: Insects, earthworms, slugs, snails, and amphibian and fish eggs
records.shelter: Under rotting logs, rocks, and leaf litter; in ponds during breeding season
records.preferredHabitat: Pacific conifer forest near still or slow water
records.fact: Its skin holds enough tetrodotoxin to kill several adults, driving a famous poison arms race with garter snakes.

requirements.hint: A mushroom log and a few flooded water tiles.

records.role: The rough-skinned newt is a mid-trophic consumer of insects, worms, and amphibian eggs, shaping wetland invertebrate and amphibian communities. Its potent tetrodotoxin defense drives adaptive evolution in resistant garter snakes, one of biology's best-known coevolutionary arms races. The toxin leaves it nearly free from most other predators.

sources.name: USGS — Barred Owl predation on Taricha granulosa

records.name: Northern Flying Squirrel
records.diet: Mostly underground truffle fungi; also lichens, seeds, nuts, fruit, and insects
records.shelter: Tree cavities, old woodpecker holes, and branch dreys; huddles in winter groups
records.preferredHabitat: Closed-canopy mature conifer forest rich in mycorrhizal fungi
records.fact: Fungal spores turn up in nearly every flying squirrel dropping, making it the forest's key truffle disperser.

requirements.hint: Nesting tree and a stump, once tree squirrels are back.

records.role: The northern flying squirrel is a keystone mutualist, the main disperser of underground mycorrhizal fungi that conifers depend on for nutrients. This squirrel-fungi-tree partnership underpins forest regeneration. It is also a prime prey item for owls, martens, and fishers, funneling energy from the fungal layer up to top predators.

sources.name: USDA Forest Service — Meyer et al. 2005 (truffle spore dispersal)

records.name: Wood Duck
records.diet: Acorns, seeds, and aquatic plants; ducklings and spring birds also eat insects and snails
records.shelter: Obligate cavity nester in tree holes and nest boxes near water
records.preferredHabitat: Bottomland hardwood and wooded swamps with slow water and cavity trees
records.fact: A day after hatching, wood duck ducklings leap from nest cavities up to 50 feet high and land unhurt.

requirements.hint: A nesting tree beside a flooded pool of 4+ water tiles.

records.role: Wood ducks are omnivorous consumers linking bottomland forest and wetland food webs, dispersing acorn and aquatic-plant seeds and regulating shallow-water invertebrates. As prey they feed great horned owls, mink, raccoons, and snapping turtles. Depending on woodpecker cavities, their abundance signals healthy wooded wetlands.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Wood Duck

records.name: American Bittern
records.diet: Fish, frogs, insects, crayfish, snakes, and small mammals
records.shelter: Platform nests hidden low in dense reeds
records.preferredHabitat: Tall marsh vegetation over shallow water
records.fact: The bittern freezes bill-skyward, swaying like a reed to vanish in the marsh.

requirements.hint: Thick reeds and cattails beside open water.

records.role: A secretive ambush predator of the reed beds. It stands motionless, then seizes fish, frogs, and insects, relying on stripy camouflage to stay hidden.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - American Bittern

records.name: Belted Kingfisher
records.diet: Small fish and crayfish, plus other aquatic prey
records.shelter: Tunnel burrows dug into earthen banks
records.preferredHabitat: Clear water with perches over fishable shallows
records.fact: Kingfishers dive headfirst into the water with their eyes closed to grab fish.

requirements.hint: Carve a river 4+ tiles long with fish present, plus a platform.

records.role: A plunge-diving fish specialist that watches from a perch and dives on small fish and crayfish. It nests in tunnels dug metres into stream banks.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - Belted Kingfisher

records.name: Northern Leopard Frog
records.diet: Insects, spiders, worms, and other small animals
records.shelter: Shallow water and grassy margins
records.preferredHabitat: Lily-fringed shallows
records.fact: Leopard frogs escape with erratic zig-zag leaps straight back into the water.

requirements.hint: A lily pool and a few open-water tiles.

records.role: A wide-mouthed generalist that eats almost any small animal it can swallow, from insects to smaller frogs. It is key prey for herons, mink, and snakes.

sources.name: U.S. National Park Service - Northern Leopard Frog

records.name: Snapping Turtle
records.diet: Fish, aquatic plants, carrion, and almost anything it can catch
records.shelter: Muddy lake and pond bottoms
records.preferredHabitat: Deep still water with a soft mud bottom
records.fact: Adult snapping turtles have almost no natural predators and can live for decades.

requirements.hint: A mud bank beside a lake of 5+ connected water tiles.

records.role: A heavily armored omnivore and scavenger lurking on the pond bottom. As an adult it sits near the top of the wetland food web, eating fish, ducklings, plants, and carrion.

records.name: Marsh Wren
records.diet: Insects and spiders picked from marsh vegetation
records.shelter: Woven dome nests among cattails and bulrushes
records.preferredHabitat: Cattail and sedge stands
records.fact: Males build many dummy nests and even destroy neighbours' eggs.

requirements.hint: Two reed beds and a sedge tussock.

records.role: A tiny, feisty insectivore of the reeds. It gleans insects and spiders from stems and famously builds several decoy nests to court a mate.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - Marsh Wren

records.name: Gila Woodpecker
records.diet: Insects, cactus fruit, and berries
records.shelter: Cavities excavated in saguaro cactus
records.preferredHabitat: Saguaro and cactus stands
records.fact: Its abandoned saguaro cavities later shelter elf owls, pygmy-owls, and kestrels.

requirements.hint: Two cactus patches for nesting cavities.

records.role: A cactus-nesting woodpecker and desert keystone builder. It eats insects, cactus fruit, and berries, and its old nest holes house many other desert animals. Hawks, snakes, and bobcats prey on it.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Gila Woodpecker

records.name: Cactus Wren
records.diet: Spiders, insects, and some fruit
records.shelter: Thorny cactus and brush
records.preferredHabitat: Open desert with cactus
records.fact: Cactus wrens use their football-shaped cholla nests year-round, even sleeping in them.

requirements.hint: A cactus patch and desert brush.

records.role: The largest North American wren, an insectivore gleaning spiders and insects and taking cactus fruit. It gets most of its water from food. Snakes, roadrunners, and hawks prey on it and its nests.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Cactus Wren

records.name: Desert Iguana
records.diet: Flowers, buds, and leaves, especially creosote
records.shelter: Burrows under shrubs
records.preferredHabitat: Hot sandy flats with cover
records.fact: Desert iguanas stay active near 40C, heat that drives other lizards into the shade.

requirements.hint: An agave rosette and a rock pile.

records.role: A heat-loving herbivorous lizard that feeds mainly on creosote bush flowers and leaves. It is a desert plant grazer and prey for snakes, raptors, and foxes. It shelters in burrows through the hottest hours.

records.name: Kangaroo Mouse
records.diet: Seeds, plus insects in summer
records.shelter: Sand burrows plugged by day
records.preferredHabitat: Fine sandy desert
records.fact: It survives on water made from its food and may go a lifetime without ever drinking.

requirements.hint: A burrow mound near desert brush.

records.role: A tiny seed-eating rodent that stores fat in its tail for lean times. It is prey for rattlesnakes, owls, and foxes, making it part of the base of the desert food web. It rarely if ever needs to drink.

records.name: Western Banded Gecko
records.diet: Insects, spiders, and small scorpions
records.shelter: Rock crevices
records.preferredHabitat: Sheltered rocky desert
records.fact: Unlike most geckos, the banded gecko has movable eyelids and squeaks when captured.

requirements.hint: Ocotillo beside a shaded rock shelter.

records.role: A small nocturnal gecko that hunts insects, spiders, and even young scorpions. It is a mesopredator on tiny desert prey and food for larger lizards, snakes, and roadrunners. It sheds its tail to escape.

sources.name: Arizona-Sonora Desert Museum — Western Banded Gecko

records.name: Gray-crowned Rosy-Finch
records.diet: Tiny alpine plant seeds and insects, often gleaned off snowfields
records.shelter: Bulky cup of moss and grass tucked into a cliff crack or talus
records.preferredHabitat: Alpine zones above treeline: talus, scree, cliffs, and glaciers
records.fact: It nests higher than nearly any other songbird in North America.

requirements.hint: Alpine wildflowers and a rock pile.

records.role: A high-altitude songbird that hops across snow and talus gathering wind-borne seeds and chilled insects. It nests in rock crevices above treeline. Falcons and hawks are its main predators.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - Gray-crowned Rosy-Finch

records.name: American Pipit
records.diet: Mostly insects and their larvae, plus spiders and some seeds
records.shelter: Ground nest of grass tucked beside a rock or vegetation clump
records.preferredHabitat: Open alpine meadows and tundra in the breeding season
records.fact: It forages at snowbank edges for insects chilled after drifting up from below.

requirements.hint: A heather mat and alpine wildflowers.

records.role: A slender ground-walking songbird of open alpine meadows that constantly bobs its tail as it hunts insects. It gleans chilled prey from snowbank margins. Hawks and nest raiders are its chief threats.

sources.name: Birds of the World - American Pipit Food Habits

records.name: Ermine
records.diet: Small rodents, especially voles; also pikas, birds, eggs, and insects
records.shelter: Dens in prey burrows, rock piles, and hollow logs, lined with fur
records.preferredHabitat: Talus and shrubby edges near meadows with dense rodent prey
records.fact: Its coat turns pure white in winter except for a jet-black tail tip.

requirements.hint: Rock pile and krummholz, once pikas are back.

records.role: A small, fierce weasel that specializes in voles and other rodents, also taking young pikas and ground-bird eggs. It hunts prey burrows it can slip right into. Foxes, martens, and raptors prey on it in turn.

sources.name: Idaho Fish and Game - Mustela erminea

records.name: Boreal Toad
records.diet: Beetles, ants, flies, and other invertebrates; tadpoles graze algae
records.shelter: Burrows, rodent holes, logs, and rocks in moist cover near pools
records.preferredHabitat: Subalpine and alpine wet meadows with open breeding pools
records.fact: Rocky Mountain boreal toads have crashed from the deadly amphibian chytrid fungus.

requirements.hint: A snowmelt pool and a few open-water tiles.

records.role: The high country's only toad, an insect-eating amphibian that breeds in shallow snowmelt pools and takes years to mature. Its tadpoles graze algae. Chytrid fungus has devastated southern populations, making it a conservation flagship.

records.name: Mountain Bluebird
records.diet: Mostly insects caught in flight; berries and seeds in colder months
records.shelter: Old woodpecker holes, natural cavities, and nest boxes
records.preferredHabitat: Open high meadows with scattered trees and hunting perches
records.fact: It cannot dig its own hole, so it reuses old woodpecker cavities and nest boxes.

requirements.hint: A krummholz pine and alpine wildflowers.

records.role: A brilliant sky-blue thrush of open high meadows that hover-hunts insects on the wing and adds berries in the cold. As a cavity nester it depends on old woodpecker holes. Hawks and cavity raiders prey on it.

records.name: Sanderling
records.diet: Small crabs, amphipods, worms, and mollusks
records.shelter: Open beach above the surf line
records.preferredHabitat: Sandy surf line and wave-washed beach
records.fact: Sanderlings chase retreating waves in busy little sprints to grab stranded invertebrates.

requirements.hint: Two dune-grass plantings and a tidepool.

records.role: A wave-chasing sandpiper that feeds on small crustaceans and worms churned up by the surf. Falcons are a key predator, and its winter flocks track the health of open sandy beaches.

sources.name: All About Birds - Sanderling Life History

records.name: Black Oystercatcher
records.diet: Mussels and limpets, plus whelks and crabs
records.shelter: Rocky shore ledges just above the tide
records.preferredHabitat: Rocky intertidal reefs and tidepool shores
records.fact: Its long red bill pries shellfish open and cuts the muscle before the shell shuts.

requirements.hint: An oyster bed beside a tidepool.

records.role: A rocky-shore specialist that pries mussels and limpets from the rocks, timing feeding to the tides. It is a sensitive indicator of intertidal health, thriving only where shellfish are plentiful.

sources.name: All About Birds - Black Oystercatcher Life History

records.name: Purple Shore Crab
records.diet: Sea lettuce and other green algae, plus occasional carrion
records.shelter: Under rocks in the intertidal
records.preferredHabitat: Sheltered rocky intertidal under stones
records.fact: They scrape green algae from rocks and scuttle sideways under stones at low tide.

requirements.hint: A tidepool and an oyster bed.

records.role: A small grazing crab that scrapes algae from intertidal rocks and occasionally scavenges. It is common prey for gulls, anemones, and tidepool fish, moving algal energy up the food web.

records.name: Brant Goose
records.diet: Eelgrass and large green algae like sea lettuce
records.shelter: Open shoreline and shallow bays
records.preferredHabitat: Shallow coastal bays with eelgrass beds
records.fact: Whole flocks of brant depend on eelgrass beds to fuel their long migrations.

requirements.hint: An eelgrass bed beside open water.

records.role: A small sea goose that grazes almost entirely on eelgrass and green algae in shallow bays. Its dependence on eelgrass makes healthy brant flocks a clear indicator of intact seagrass beds.

sources.name: All About Birds - Brant Life History

records.name: Western Snowy Plover
records.diet: Beach invertebrates: crustaceans, flies, and small mollusks
records.shelter: Shallow scrapes on open sand
records.preferredHabitat: Quiet sandy dunes and open beach
records.fact: Western snowy plovers nest in tiny scrapes right on the open sand.

requirements.hint: Dune grass and a coastal nesting area.

records.role: A threatened beach-nesting plover that feeds on small invertebrates along the sand and tide line. Extremely sensitive to disturbance, it is a flagship indicator of protected, undisturbed dune beaches.

sources.name: All About Birds - Snowy Plover Life History

records.name: Costa's Hummingbird
records.diet: Flower nectar and tiny insects
records.shelter: Nests in shrubs and cactus
records.preferredHabitat: Blooming desert with nectar sources
records.fact: Courting males dive past a female with a shrill whistle, flashing violet throat feathers.

requirements.hint: A nectar feeder beside a cactus patch.

records.role: A small desert hummingbird that feeds on nectar from agave, chuparosa, and other blooms plus tiny insects. It is an important pollinator and a nectar-feeding herbivore. Snakes and predatory birds take it.

records.name: Cooper's Hawk
records.diet: Mainly medium and small birds; also chipmunks, mice, and squirrels
records.shelter: Builds a stick nest high in a tree, on a limb or in a crotch
records.preferredHabitat: Woodland edges and open country with scattered trees near meadows
records.fact: Cooper's Hawks thread through dense cover at high speed to ambush songbirds — a risky style that leaves many with healed chest-bone fractures.

requirements.hint: Plant an oak, add a bird perch and a shrub, once sparrows are back.

records.role: A bird-hunting mesopredator that patrols meadow edges and thickets for songbirds. Its agile, low pursuit flight lets it pluck sparrows, finches, and bluebirds from cover. It controls small-bird numbers but can itself be displaced by larger raptors.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Cooper's Hawk Life History
Cornell Lab All About Birds — Cooper's Hawk Overview

records.name: Western Screech-Owl
records.diet: Small mammals and large insects; also small birds and worms
records.shelter: Roosts and nests in tree cavities, old woodpecker holes, and boxes
records.preferredHabitat: Wooded edges and brushy areas bordering open meadows
records.fact: This pint-sized owl occasionally takes prey larger than itself, including cottontail rabbits.

requirements.hint: Plant an oak and craft a hollow log and log shelter.

records.role: A small nocturnal mesopredator that sits and waits, then drops onto rodents and insects, gleaning grasshoppers and beetles and snatching voles and mice on the ground. It bridges insect and rodent control in the meadow at night.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Western Screech-Owl Life History
Cornell Lab All About Birds — Western Screech-Owl Overview

records.name: Barred Owl
records.diet: Small mammals, birds, amphibians, reptiles, fish, and invertebrates
records.shelter: Large tree cavities in mature forest; also old hawk, crow, or squirrel nests
records.preferredHabitat: Mature mixed or conifer forest near water with large cavity trees
records.fact: Barred owls sometimes wade into shallow water to catch fish—unusual hunting for a woodland owl.

requirements.hint: A nesting tree, a planted oak, and standing deadwood.

records.role: The barred owl is a mid-level predator that regulates mice, voles, chipmunks, squirrels, and amphibians. It sits between small prey and the apex great horned owl, which is its main predator. Its need for large cavity trees makes it an indicator of mature forest health.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Barred Owl

records.name: Fisher
records.diet: Small and medium mammals—porcupines, hares, squirrels, mice; also birds and fruit
records.shelter: Dens in hollow trees, logs, stumps, and ground burrows; young in high tree cavities
records.preferredHabitat: Dense conifer and mixed forest with high canopy closure and hollow trees
records.fact: The fisher is one of the only predators that regularly kills porcupines, slashing the face until it can flip it over.

requirements.hint: Plant a birch, add a stump and mushroom log, once squirrels are back.

records.role: The fisher is a powerful mid-level forest predator and one of the few checks on porcupine numbers, which otherwise damage timber. It partly fills the niche of vanished apex predators, and its presence signals mature, connected forest. Young fishers are prey for bobcats, foxes, and lynx.

records.name: Prothonotary Warbler
records.diet: Insects and spiders; some snails, fruit, and seeds off-season
records.shelter: Tree cavities and nest boxes over standing water
records.preferredHabitat: Flooded wooded swamp
records.fact: It is one of only two North American warblers that nest in tree cavities.

requirements.hint: Plant a bald cypress with a reed bed and nesting platform.

records.role: A glowing-gold swamp warbler that gleans insects and spiders over the water. Unusually for a warbler, it nests in cavities, often above standing water.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - Prothonotary Warbler

records.name: Green Heron
records.diet: Mainly small fish; also insects, crustaceans, and frogs
records.shelter: Stick nests in trees and shrubs overhanging water
records.preferredHabitat: Quiet wooded shallows
records.fact: The green heron drops bait on the water to lure fish within striking range.

requirements.hint: Plant a water tupelo by a lily pool and open water.

records.role: A small, crafty heron of shady shallows and one of few tool-using birds. It fishes patiently and sometimes baits the surface to draw fish close.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - Green Heron

records.name: Elf Owl
records.diet: Insects and scorpions
records.shelter: Cavities in cactus and trees
records.preferredHabitat: Mesquite and saguaro desert
records.fact: The world's smallest owl plucks the stinger off scorpions before eating them.

requirements.hint: Plant a mesquite and an ironwood beside a cactus patch.

records.role: The world's smallest owl, a nocturnal insectivore that hunts insects and scorpions and nests in old woodpecker holes. It is a mesopredator on desert arthropods. Snakes and larger owls threaten it.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Elf Owl
Cornell Lab All About Birds — Elf Owl Overview

records.name: Mountain Chickadee
records.diet: Insects and spiders in summer; conifer seeds and nuts in fall and winter
records.shelter: Old woodpecker holes and natural cavities in conifers and aspen
records.preferredHabitat: High evergreen forests of pine, fir, and spruce in the West
records.fact: It caches thousands of seeds and remembers where it hid them.

requirements.hint: Plant a subalpine fir and krummholz with alpine wildflowers.

records.role: A busy conifer-forest insectivore that gleans insects from twigs and switches to cached pine seeds in winter. Often the nucleus of mixed foraging flocks, it disperses conifer seeds. Small hawks, weasels, and martens prey on it and its nestlings.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - Mountain Chickadee

records.name: Pine Grosbeak
records.diet: Buds, seeds, and fruits of conifers and shrubs; some insects in summer
records.shelter: Concealed cup nest near the trunk of a dense conifer
records.preferredHabitat: Open subalpine spruce, fir, and pine forest near timberline
records.fact: A plump, unhurried finch of the cold high forests, nipping buds and needles.

requirements.hint: Plant an aspen and a subalpine fir near a rock pile.

records.role: A large, sluggish finch that lives almost entirely on conifer buds, seeds, and fruits, adding insects to feed its young. It helps disperse tree and shrub seeds. Martens, small raptors, and foxes prey on it, especially at nests.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - Pine Grosbeak

records.name: Anna's Hummingbird
records.diet: Flower nectar and small insects
records.shelter: Shrubs and small trees in coastal scrub
records.preferredHabitat: Flowering coastal scrub and gardens
records.fact: Males dive from about 27 m and pull up with a loud chirp made by their tail feathers.

requirements.hint: Plant a Monterey cypress with dune grass and sea thrift.

records.role: A year-round coastal hummingbird that feeds on nectar and small insects, pollinating shrubs like manzanita and gooseberry as it forages. It links flowering coastal scrub to the wider food web.

sources.name: All About Birds - Anna's Hummingbird Life History

records.name: Acorn Woodpecker
records.diet: Acorns and insects, plus sap and fruit
records.shelter: Oak granary trees with stored acorns
records.preferredHabitat: Coastal oak woodland
records.fact: It drills thousands of holes in a granary tree and stores a single acorn in each.

requirements.hint: Plant a coast live oak near a driftwood shelter and tidepool.

records.role: A social woodpecker that hoards acorns in shared granary trees and hawks flying insects. Its acorn caching and old cavities support other coastal-woodland animals, making it a habitat keystone in oak groves.

sources.name: All About Birds - Acorn Woodpecker Life History

records.name: Praying Mantis
records.diet: Ambush predator eating live insects — bees, grasshoppers, and more
records.shelter: Perches motionless on plants; lays eggs in a foam egg case (ootheca)
records.preferredHabitat: Meadows and shrubby edges with dense vegetation for ambush
records.fact: A praying mantis can swivel its head almost 180 degrees — unique among insects — for a wide field of view.

requirements.hint: Tall grass, a shrub, and an insect hotel give it cover to hunt from.

records.role: A sit-and-wait ambush mesopredator that seizes prey with spined forelegs in a strike faster than a blink. As a generalist it eats grasshoppers, bees, beetles, and other insects, helping regulate insect numbers. It is itself taken by birds, garter snakes, and small owls.

records.name: Killdeer
records.diet: Invertebrates — earthworms, grasshoppers, beetles, and snails
records.shelter: Nests in a bare ground scrape lined with pebbles and shell bits
records.preferredHabitat: Open, flat ground with very short grass and scattered stones
records.fact: Killdeer fake a broken wing, dragging it as if injured to lure predators away from the nest.

requirements.hint: Open native grass with a rock pile and a stone wall to nest beside.

records.role: A ground-foraging insectivore that races and halts across open meadow, snapping up worms and insects. As abundant, exposed ground-nesters they are important prey for meadow hunters, which take adults, chicks, and eggs alike.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Killdeer Life History

records.name: Red Admiral
records.diet: Adults prefer tree sap, fermenting fruit, and nectar; caterpillars eat nettles
records.shelter: Caterpillars fold nettle leaves into shelters; adults roost on trees
records.preferredHabitat: Flowery clearings and woodland edges near nettle patches
records.fact: Red admirals are bold and territorial, and will readily land and perch on people who stay still.

requirements.hint: Butterfly flowers and wildflowers beside an insect hotel.

records.role: A fast, territorial butterfly that feeds mainly on tree sap, fruit, and dung, visiting flowers as a nectar pollinator when preferred foods are scarce; its caterpillars specialize on stinging nettles. Lacking chemical defenses, it relies on camouflage and speed to escape birds and other predators.

sources.name: USDA Forest Service — Red Admiral Butterfly
Butterflies and Moths of North America — Red Admiral

records.name: Little Brown Bat
records.diet: Strict insectivore: midges, caddisflies, mayflies, moths, beetles, and mosquitoes
records.shelter: Roosts in tree hollows, under bark, and in buildings; hibernates in caves and mines
records.preferredHabitat: Forested land near streams, ponds, and openings for aerial feeding
records.fact: White-nose syndrome, a cold-loving fungus, has wiped out over 90% of little brown bats at many hibernation sites.

requirements.hint: A bat box near standing deadwood, with shrubs full of insects.

records.role: Little brown bats are voracious insectivores, each eating up to half its body weight in insects a night and suppressing forest and aquatic pests. They are a mid-web link between the insect layer and larger predators like owls, fishers, and snakes. White-nose syndrome has caused catastrophic declines.

records.name: Ensatina Salamander
records.diet: Invertebrates: worms, ants, beetles, spiders, centipedes, millipedes, and snails
records.shelter: Under rocks, bark, and logs on the forest floor; retreats underground when dry
records.preferredHabitat: Moist, shaded forest floor rich in coarse woody debris
records.fact: Ensatinas are lungless, breathing through their skin, and can drop a wriggling, poison-laced tail to escape.

requirements.hint: Leaf litter and a mushroom log beside a shallow pool.

records.role: The ensatina is an abundant forest-floor predator that suppresses decomposer invertebrates like centipedes, millipedes, and sowbugs, linking the detritus web to vertebrate predators. Being lungless, it depends on damp, intact forest, making it an indicator of forest-floor moisture. It is prey for garter snakes, raccoons, and jays.

records.name: Spotted Towhee
records.diet: Insects and invertebrates in summer; seeds, acorns, and berries in fall and winter
records.shelter: Dense shrubby thickets and brushy edges; nests on or near the ground
records.preferredHabitat: Brushy forest edges and chaparral with deep leaf litter
records.fact: The spotted towhee feeds with a two-footed backward hop that flicks leaf litter aside to expose food.

requirements.hint: A brush pile and shrubs over a bed of leaf litter.

records.role: The spotted towhee is an omnivorous ground forager that bridges the invertebrate and seed layers, eating ground beetles and caterpillars in summer and dispersing seeds in winter. Its ground nesting leaves it vulnerable to foxes, raccoons, and snakes, while hawks and owls take adults. It helps turn over and recycle forest-floor litter.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Spotted Towhee

records.name: Hooded Merganser
records.diet: Small fish, crayfish, aquatic insects, and amphibians
records.shelter: Tree cavities and nest boxes near water
records.preferredHabitat: Quiet wooded ponds
records.fact: Hooded merganser ducklings can dive for their own food at just one day old.

requirements.hint: A duck nest box beside reeds and open water.

records.role: A small diving duck with a serrated bill for gripping slippery prey. It pursues fish, crayfish, and insects underwater and nests in tree cavities.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - Hooded Merganser

records.name: Spotted Turtle
records.diet: Aquatic plants, insects, worms, mollusks, and small invertebrates
records.shelter: Basking logs and shallow, muddy-bottomed water
records.preferredHabitat: Sunny shallow marsh
records.fact: Each spotted turtle wears a unique pattern of yellow polka dots on its shell.

requirements.hint: A basking log in a reedy, shallow pool.

records.role: A small, declining omnivore that forages underwater for plants and invertebrates. It basks on logs and buries in mud when startled.

sources.name: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service - Spotted Turtle

records.name: Common Yellowthroat
records.diet: Insects and spiders gleaned from low vegetation
records.shelter: Bulky grass cups low in cattails and sedges
records.preferredHabitat: Thick marsh vegetation
records.fact: The male's black bandit mask is a signal that rivals will attack on sight.

requirements.hint: A cattail stand among thick reed beds.

records.role: A masked marsh warbler that gleans insects and spiders from dense low cover. It skulks through cattails and briars in search of prey.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - Common Yellowthroat

records.name: Chuckwalla
records.diet: Desert flowers, leaves, and fruit
records.shelter: Rock crevices
records.preferredHabitat: Boulder piles near brush
records.fact: A threatened chuckwalla wedges into a crack and inflates its lungs to lock itself in.

requirements.hint: A rock crevice to wedge into, with cactus and brush to graze — and a sun-warmed cairn to bask on.

records.role: A large herbivorous lizard that grazes desert leaves, flowers, and fruit among boulders. It is a plant-eater and prey for hawks, kestrels, coyotes, and rattlesnakes. Its lung-inflation defense locks it into crevices.

records.name: Phainopepla
records.diet: Mistletoe berries and flying insects
records.shelter: Tall desert brush
records.preferredHabitat: Brushy desert with water nearby
records.fact: The phainopepla is desert mistletoe's key seed disperser; the two depend on each other.

requirements.hint: Dense desert brush beside a dew basin.

records.role: A glossy desert songbird whose winter diet is mostly desert mistletoe berries, plus insects caught on the wing. It is a crucial mistletoe seed disperser and a fruit-and-insect omnivore. Snakes and raptors prey on it.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Phainopepla

records.name: Antelope Squirrel
records.diet: Seeds, fruit, greens, and insects
records.shelter: Burrows and rock cracks
records.preferredHabitat: Open desert with burrows
records.fact: It carries its tail arched over its back like a parasol to shade itself from the sun.

requirements.hint: A burrow and a rock crevice among desert brush.

records.role: A diurnal, heat-tolerant omnivore that eats seeds, greens, fruit, and insects even in midday heat. It is prey for hawks, foxes, bobcats, and snakes. It shades itself with its tail and dumps heat on cool ground.

records.name: Alpine Chipmunk
records.diet: Seeds of sedges, forbs, and grasses, plus berries, fungi, pine seeds, and eggs
records.shelter: Nests deep in crevices between talus rocks and boulders
records.preferredHabitat: High talus slopes and rocky meadows of the Sierra Nevada
records.fact: It ranges higher than almost any other chipmunk, up to 3,900 meters.

requirements.hint: A talus pile and rock pile among alpine wildflowers.

records.role: A tiny, high-altitude seed-eater that caches seeds and helps disperse alpine plants across the talus. It also raids the eggs of rosy-finches and sparrows. Foxes, weasels, martens, and raptors all hunt it, tying it into the predator web.

records.name: White-crowned Sparrow
records.diet: Mainly weed and grass seeds, plus caterpillars, beetles, and other insects
records.shelter: Ground or low-shrub cup nest among mosses, lichens, and heath
records.preferredHabitat: Krummholz edges, alpine meadows, and heath with bare ground
records.fact: Young white-crowns learn their song dialect from the neighbours nearby.

requirements.hint: A heather mat and nest shelf sheltered by krummholz pine.

records.role: A ground-foraging sparrow of alpine meadow and krummholz edges that eats seeds and summer insects. It disperses seeds and feeds insect larvae to its chicks. Foxes, weasels, and martens hunt the adults and raid its low nests.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - White-crowned Sparrow

records.name: Cascades Frog
records.diet: An aquatic and semiaquatic insectivore, taking insects and spiders
records.shelter: Snowmelt ponds and lakes; hibernates in soil under lake bottoms
records.preferredHabitat: Cold high-country ponds and streams near coniferous forest
records.fact: It stays active in near-freezing snowmelt water and basks on wet rocks.

requirements.hint: A snowmelt pool beside a talus pile, with open water near.

records.role: A cold-adapted mountain frog that eats insects and spiders while its tadpoles graze algae in snowmelt pools. It links pond invertebrates to larger predators. Introduced trout eat its tadpoles, driving steep declines across its southern range.

records.name: Black Turnstone
records.diet: Barnacles, limpets, mussels, and small invertebrates
records.shelter: Rocky shoreline and beach wrack
records.preferredHabitat: Rocky intertidal shores
records.fact: Turnstones flip over stones and shells to snatch the creatures hiding beneath.

requirements.hint: Tidepools and kelp wrack with a driftwood pile to shelter in.

records.role: A rocky-shore forager that pries barnacles and limpets loose and flips wrack to find hidden prey. It helps keep intertidal invertebrate numbers in check and depends on rich rocky shores.

sources.name: All About Birds - Black Turnstone Life History

records.name: Pigeon Guillemot
records.diet: Small fish, plus crabs, worms, and mollusks
records.shelter: Bluff and rock crevices above water
records.preferredHabitat: Rocky nesting bluffs over clear water
records.fact: Pigeon guillemots have bright coral-red feet and matching mouth linings.

requirements.hint: A nesting bluff above open water near an oyster bed.

records.role: A diving seabird that chases small fish and pries invertebrates from crevices near the seafloor. It nests in rocky bluffs and depends on the healthy nearshore fish and habitat that kelp forests support.

sources.name: All About Birds - Pigeon Guillemot Life History

records.name: Bat Star
records.diet: Algae, detritus, and dead plants and animals
records.shelter: Tidepools and eelgrass beds
records.preferredHabitat: Shallow rocky tidepools and eelgrass
records.fact: A bat star can have anywhere from four to nine arms, not always five.

requirements.hint: A couple of tidepools with an eelgrass bed.

records.role: An omnivorous scavenger that spreads its stomach over the seafloor to digest algae and carrion. It is a cleanup crew of the shallows, recycling dead matter and keeping tidepools and eelgrass beds tidy.
